newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian army expects wages but says problems acute.
newsitem.headline: Russian army expects wages but says problems acute.

text.p: The Russian military's chief financial officer said on Thursday that servicemen would receive months of unpaid wages by September, but cautioned that the armed forces' financial problems remained acute.

Lieutenant-General Georgy Oleinik, head of the armed forces main directorate for budget and finance, said he was sure the government would carry out an order by President Boris Yeltsin to settle the military wage debt in the next two months.
Encouraged by the government's recent success in paying off pensions, Yeltsin has made settling the demoralised armed forces' wage problems his government's next priority task.
"If this debt is wiped out, and I am sure it will be, then our servicemen will receive their wage arrears by September 1 -- in the time planned," Oleinik told a news conference.

He said the back wages, totalling 8.1 trillion roubles ($1.4 billion), would be paid in three stages -- first to problem areas such northern Russia and the Far East, then to soldiers on active combat and finally to less demanding areas.

He said the government would also gradually settle other debts to servicemen, including unpaid child and food allowances, by the end of the year. All the money would come out of state coffers, not directly from the military, he said.
But Oleinik said the armed forces were not receiving all the funds they are entitled to under the budget.

The government initially set aside 88.3 trillion ($15.3 billion) for the armed forces in 1997 but later reduced the amount to 67.2 trillion ($11.6 billion) under budget cuts. The military have so far received 22 trillion ($3.8 billion).
"The state of financing in the armed forces remains extremely difficult," he said. "You understand that reform of the armed forces is only possible if financing issues are addressed."
The armed forces were once Moscow's pride and joy but have fallen on hard times since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Some soldiers have not been paid for months, morale is low and the armed forces were humiliated in a nearly 21-month war with Chechen separatists which ended last August.
Yeltsin plans to reduce manpower in the armed forces from about 1.5 million to 1.2 million next year, but military reform has long been stalled and the debate over financing rages on.

A defence expert, producing yet more proposals for reform on behalf of the advisory Council on Foreign and Defence Policy, said Russia was coming to a make-or-break point after five years of dawdling over reforms and underfinancing the army.

Alexei Arbatov, deputy head of parliament's defence committee, said Yeltsin's proposed manpower cuts would be possible only if funds for the down-scaling were provided in addition to the budget spending.

"A number of crisis signs have now appeared...which show we are coming to a turning point, the consequences of which will be either a ruinous destruction of what is left or a turn for the better," Arbatov told a separate news conference.
